task.name: A spike can close without producing either a recorded decision or a follow-on work item, so its result survives only in operator memory
task.story_text:
A spike can close without producing either a recorded decision or a follow-on work item, so its result survives only in operator memory

## Problem

A spike is chartered to answer a question — whether an approach is worth adopting — and its
deliverables are a design document and a validating POC. Nothing requires it to end in a
statement of what happens next.

#2348 is the concrete case. It shipped a working POC that ranks modules by controlled excess
spend, together with a comparison hook whose purpose is to let the approach visibly fail. Run
today it reports its trust threshold unmet and declines to be used. The spike is closed. There
is no recorded decision to adopt, no recorded decision to reject, and until #2599 was filed by
hand there was no artifact naming the condition under which the question becomes answerable.

The failure mode is not that the work was wasted. It is that the result decays into nothing
without anyone noticing: a closed spike and an un-run POC look, six weeks later, exactly like
a spike that was never chartered. The only thing standing between the two is whether an
operator happens to remember, which is the property the rest of the pipeline is built to
avoid depending on.

This generalises past #2348. Any spike whose answer is "not yet", "it depends", or "promising
but unproven" has the same shape, and those are the most common honest answers a spike
produces. A spike that concludes cleanly in either direction is the easy case.

## Acceptance criteria

- A spike cannot reach a closed state without one of two recorded outcomes: a decision not to
  proceed, captured with its reasoning, or a follow-on work item that exists in the pipeline
  and is visible in the same places other work is visible.
- Where the spike's answer is conditional, the condition is carried by the follow-on artifact
  rather than by prose in the closed spike — including what would have to be true, and how an
  operator or the system would know it had become true.
- The requirement is enforced where a spike is closed, not offered as guidance a closing
  operator may follow.
- Nothing here obliges a spike to recommend proceeding. "Do not do this" is a complete and
  successful outcome, and is recorded as one rather than as an absence.

## Example

The two legal exits from a spike:

| outcome | what must exist afterwards |
|---|---|
| do not proceed | a recorded decision on the spike, naming why, so the question is closed rather than dropped |
| proceed, or proceed when X | a follow-on issue in the pipeline, carrying the trigger condition if there is one |
| *(nothing)* | not a legal exit |

#2348's actual exit was the third row: a closed spike, a POC that declines to be used, and the
condition for re-asking recorded nowhere.

handoff.summary: Made `spike` a first-class issue type in the declarative issue specification, then centralized the two-legal-exits rule in a new `theforge.spike_guard` package: `outcome.py` holds the pure stdlib rule (marker parsing, do_not_proceed/follow_up/conditional_follow_up validation, follow-on pipeline checks, trigger-condition parsing), `guard.py` is the `gh` boundary that fetches the spike, its comments and the follow-on issue, and `__main__.py` exposes `python -m theforge.spike_guard <issue>` for workflows (exit 0 = may close, 2 = refused with the reason on stderr). Every close path now calls the guard immediately before `gh issue close`: GitHubIssueSource's merged-land close and both ALREADY_DONE dispositions (routed through one `_may_close_issue` helper that also keeps the would-be closing comment durable when the close is refused), `forge todo` triage, triage ratification's `_gh_issue_close`, `close-on-merge.yml`, and `close-epic-on-last-subissue.yml`. A spike's PR body emits `Refs #N` instead of `Closes #N` so GitHub's native default-branch auto-close cannot decide the question before the guard runs. Because GitHub offers no synchronous pre-close hook, a new `enforce-spike-outcome.yml` runs on `issues.closed`, re-asks the same guard, and reopens the spike with the reason when the close was not a legal exit. A non-spike is unaffected and, on the sprint path, costs no extra `gh` call at all.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Nothing here obliges a spike to recommend proceeding. "Do not do this" is a complete and successful outcome, and is recorded as one rather than as an absence.
acceptance_criteria.notes: `do_not_proceed` is a first-class outcome kind that closes the spike on its own, requiring only its reasoning; the refusal message and the authoring guide both state that it is a complete and successful outcome.

story_deviations: The plan deferred the manual-web-UI-close hole to a follow-up; both plan reviewers flagged that AC3 asks for enforcement rather than guidance. Implemented `enforce-spike-outcome.yml` in this story instead of deferring it — it reuses the same guard entrypoint and is label-gated in the event payload.

The plan named `GitHubIssueSource.on_complete` as one close site; there are three (the merged-land close plus both `_resolve_already_done_issue` dispositions), so all three route through a shared `_may_close_issue` helper as the reviewers suggested.
The plan omitted `close-epic-on-last-subissue.yml`; it is now guarded too, since that workflow never checks the parent carries the `epic` type.

Added a `Refs #N`-not-`Closes #N` rule for spike PRs in `coordinator/completion.py`, which the plan did not cover — without it a default-branch merge auto-closes the spike natively before `on_complete` ever runs.

plan_review.findings:
- [P1-impl] [openai-gpt-5.6-sol-cli] Step 3 guards GitHubIssueSource.on_complete only after landing, but src/theforge/coordinator/completion.py:_create_pr emits Closes #N; a PR merged into the default branch is closed natively by GitHub before on_complete runs. This repository defaults workspace.base_branch to main and uses on_approve: merge-pr, making this the normal landing path.

- [P1-impl] [openai-gpt-5.6-sol-cli] The plan omits .github/workflows/close-epic-on-last-subissue.yml, which directly runs gh issue close at line 84. Despite its name, the workflow never checks the parent's labels, so any open parent—including a spike—can be closed when its last sub-issue closes.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
